sub_sections.title: Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art)
sub_sections.content:
1.1 Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives

Pertinence and framing. FIELDWISE addresses a problem of direct European relevance — water scarcity and rising climatic variability are intensifying the need for more efficient irrigation management in high-value horticulture, while irrigation decisions are still frequently based on delayed visual symptoms, isolated sensor thresholds or retrospective crop-performance information. It pursues this through the researcher-centred logic of the MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026 call (HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01). The action is a European Postdoctoral Fellowship of 30 months, hosted at HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont (ATK), Martonvásár, Hungary, and carried out by the experienced researcher Dr. Rositsa Cholakova. Its research and innovation objectives are pertinent on two axes simultaneously. Scientifically, they close three focused gaps: the physiological grounding of plant water-stress indicators (spectral and environmental variables are too often treated as stress proxies without demonstrating that they track an actual plant response); transferability across unseen conditions, sensing scales and horticultural crops; and irrigation decision relevance. In instrument terms, the same objectives are the vehicle through which the fellow completes a documented transition from plant physiologist and agronomist toward an independent Agricultural Data Scientist, acquiring the interdisciplinary (plant-stress physiology combined with agricultural data science and with hyperspectral, UAV and Earth-observation methods) and inter-sectoral competences that the call's expected outcomes explicitly seek. The proposal deliberately draws its evidence base from an existing five-season archive rather than a new campaign, and channels its inter-sectoral exposure through an integral end-of-project non-academic placement, so that its scientific and career objectives reinforce one another rather than compete.

The four objectives. The scientific programme is organised around one central challenge — whether a water-stress signal discovered in a data-rich processing-tomato system can remain biologically meaningful across seasons and sensing scales, survive prospective validation under real farmer conditions, and be encoded in a crop-configurable decision-support framework that can later be adapted to other irrigated high-value horticultural crops. This challenge is operationalised as four objectives. O1 is to "Harmonise the heterogeneous 2022-2026 MATE archive and define a physiologically meaningful water-stress target". O2 is to "Develop a parsimonious, interpretable and uncertainty-aware predictive framework under HUN-REN supervision, with ELTE spectral/EO harmonisation, and separate reusable system components from crop-specific biological/calibration parameters". O3 is to "Prospectively validate the framework at an independent commercial farmer site equipped with project meteorological and soil sensing, supported by physiological, proximal, UAV and Sentinel observations". O4 is to "Operationalise validated outputs in a crop-configurable DrR architecture through continuous Krumatic software development and AgroVIR requirements feedback, followed by industrial evaluation in M25-M30". Processing tomato is chosen as the model crop precisely because approximately five years of heterogeneous data, strong experimental expertise and established collaborations already exist for it; it is the scientifically justified starting point, not the intended limit of the technology.

Measurable and verifiable. Each objective is defined by concrete, checkable outputs rather than by aspiration, and each is anchored to a dated project deliverable so that an evaluator (and later a reviewer) can verify achievement. O1 delivers a QC-controlled common-variable matrix, a missingness/measurement-frequency map, and a target and validation protocol — captured in the harmonised database and variable-availability map (D1.1, month 14) and the Stress-target, feature-selection and validation protocol (D1.2, month 14). O2 delivers a ranked predictor set, a primary model with a nonlinear benchmark where justified, a calibration/uncertainty assessment, a model card and a crop-transfer specification — captured in the Primary model, benchmark and model card (D2.1, month 3) and the Spectral/UAV/Sentinel harmonisation and crop-transfer specification (D2.2, month 14). O3 delivers a prospective validation dataset, an unseen-environment benchmark, a spatial scaling assessment and a limited-recalibration protocol if required — captured in the Independent commercial-field validation dataset (D3.1, month 18) and the Prospective transferability, uncertainty and limited-recalibration report (D3.2, month 18). O4 delivers a web MVP with a validated processing-tomato module, an irrigation-attention output, a crop-extension specification, an AgroVIR requirements/interoperability report and a post-MSCA integration and exploitation roadmap — captured in the Crop-configurable DrR web MVP with validated processing-tomato module (D4.1, month 24), the AgroVIR operational/interoperability assessment (D5.1, month 30) and the Post-MSCA FMIS integration and exploitation roadmap (D5.2, month 30). Verifiability is reinforced by an explicit evaluation discipline: model performance is judged under blocked, leakage-safe unseen-year validation against a pre-specified physiological stress target, using pre-registered metrics — balanced accuracy, F1 and ROC-AUC for classified stress detection; RMSE, MAE and R² for continuous prediction; reliability diagrams, the Brier score and prediction-interval coverage probability for calibration; and stress-detection lead time and per-season false-alarm rate for operational value — with literature-derived acceptance thresholds fixed in D1.2 before the prospective season, and with the primary model frozen and its model card registered (D2.1) before the first field season. Pre-committing thresholds and freezing the model before validation converts each objective into a falsifiable, auditable claim rather than a moving target.

Realistically achievable. The objectives are ambitious yet grounded in resources that already exist. O1 and O2 rest on the 2022-2026 MATE processing-tomato archive (physiological, soil, meteorological and proximal spectral observations) and are developed under HUN-REN ATK supervision (primary supervisor Prof. Tibor Janda) with ELTE spectral/EO harmonisation and UAV/hyperspectral instrumentation. O3 is a single, focused prospective test at an independent commercial farmer field instrumented by the project (meteorological station and soil sensors) — the minimum that the prospective-validation logic requires — with a defined site-contingency ladder so that the transferability claim is protected. O4 builds on the fellow's pre-existing, self-financed research tool DrR - Digital Agronomist, currently a sensor/EO monitoring and data-integration tool rather than a validated advisory product, used as a research-to-application vehicle: only validated scientific components are incrementally incorporated, Krumatic supports software engineering from project start, and AgroVIR provides requirements-oriented consultation from the outset before hosting the M25-M30 placement. The scope is bounded honestly — validation within the action is limited to processing tomato, and the crop-transfer specification defines the components, parameters, minimum datasets and recalibration gates any later crop must pass — while the concrete follow-on route to additional cultivars and Bulgarian production conditions is placed after the action through MVCRI, with no in-action MVCRI effort claimed. This bounding is itself a realism argument: the fellowship promises only what its data, timeline and consortium can deliver.

Beyond the state of the art and extent of ambition. FIELDWISE is ambitious because it connects biological truth, rigorous transferability testing, sensing scale and operational decision support within a single validation chain, while deliberately designing the resulting digital framework for reuse beyond the development crop. It explicitly refuses four assumptions that are common in the field: that a vegetation index is equivalent to water stress; that proximal and satellite indices are interchangeable; that internal cross-validation proves field transferability; and that one tomato-trained model can be transferred unchanged to another horticultural crop. Its advance over current practice is expressed as seven concrete transitions: (1) from a stress proxy to a physiologically defined stress target; (2) from a heterogeneous five-season archive to an explicit common-variable/missingness design; (3) from internal fit to blocked unseen-year validation to independent commercial-field validation; (4) from leaf/proximal sensing through an ELTE hyperspectral/UAV bridge to Sentinel-2 field-scale operational inputs; (5) from a standalone model to a continuously developed DrR web MVP with AgroVIR industrial evaluation; (6) from academic-only validation to a farmer-facing real-world test plus a defined post-MSCA Bulgarian replication route through MVCRI; and (7) from a tomato-specific prototype to a crop-configurable high-value-horticulture framework with explicit crop-specific validation/calibration gates. The genuine novelty is not a new machine-learning algorithm — the deliberate methodological stance is parsimony and interpretability, avoiding a deep-learning dependency — but the construction and demonstration of a validation framework in which operationally obtainable data streams are judged against independent plant-level ground truth, challenged under both unseen-year and new commercial-field conditions, translated across sensing scales without assuming equivalence, and then separated into a reusable decision-support core and crop-specific biological/calibration components. This moves crop-stress modelling beyond retrospective predictive accuracy toward demonstrated physiological validity, transferability and management relevance, which is where the field's current weakness lies and where the project's ambition is concentrated.

sub_sections.title: Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)
sub_sections.content:
## 1.2 Soundness of the proposed methodology

### Overall methodology: concepts, models and assumptions

The methodological spine of FIELDWISE is a single, disciplined validation chain that carries one physiologically grounded water-stress signal from a heterogeneous multi-season evidence base, through leakage-safe modelling, to prospective testing under real commercial conditions and finally into an operational decision-support prototype. The design is deliberately not organised around inventing a new machine-learning algorithm; its methodological stance is parsimony, interpretability and uncertainty-awareness, and it explicitly avoids a deep-learning dependency. The unifying concept is that a model is only useful for irrigation if it has been judged against four linked criteria at once — physiological validity, predictive performance, transferability to unseen conditions, and management relevance — rather than against retrospective accuracy alone. This four-criterion evaluation frame is the organising idea from which every methodological choice below is derived.

The work rests on an explicit and falsifiable model of the underlying biology, stated as four working hypotheses. H1 (physiological-signature hypothesis) assumes that declining soil-water availability and increasing atmospheric demand produce coordinated plant responses that can be captured by a parsimonious subset of proximal spectral and environmental indicators. H2 (transferability hypothesis) assumes that predictive performance will degrade when moving from internal fitting to unseen-year and independent commercial-field validation, but that a stable core of the physiology-to-prediction workflow can nonetheless be identified and separated from crop-specific components. H3 (scale-transition hypothesis) assumes that physiologically meaningful proximal signatures will not map one-to-one onto satellite bands, but that a subset of relationships survives explicit hyperspectral/UAV-to-Sentinel harmonisation at spatial scales where field geometry supports valid Earth-observation interpretation. H4 (operational-relevance hypothesis) assumes that a model selected for physiological validity, calibration, uncertainty and stability will provide more useful irrigation-attention information than one selected solely for retrospective accuracy. Stating these as hypotheses, rather than as design assertions, is itself a methodological commitment: each is testable and each can fail visibly.

Concretely, the model to be built learns the relationship between operationally obtainable predictors — soil-water, meteorological and spectral/Earth-observation variables — and an independently measured physiological water-stress target. Defining that target is the first methodological act and the foundation of everything that follows. Rather than treating a vegetation index or an environmental threshold as a stress proxy, the project harmonises the existing 2022-2026 processing-tomato archive into a QC-controlled common-variable matrix with an explicit missingness and measurement-frequency map, and fixes a physiologically meaningful stress target and validation protocol before any model fitting. This is captured in the Harmonised database/metadata and variable-availability map and the Stress-target, feature-selection and validation protocol, and it directly delivers Objective O1. A pre-specified stress-target hierarchy is fixed in the Stress-target, feature-selection and validation protocol before model training, so that any substitution forced by the archive audit is made and documented before results are inspected, never after.

The predictive framework itself (Objective O2) is developed to be parsimonious, interpretable and uncertainty-aware: a ranked predictor set, a primary model with a single nonlinear benchmark only where justified, an explicit calibration and uncertainty assessment, and a model card. Two methodological safeguards convert each objective into an auditable claim rather than a moving target. First, model selection and evaluation are performed under blocked, leakage-safe unseen-year temporal validation, so that year-, treatment- or site-specific correlations cannot masquerade as generalisation. Second, evaluation uses pre-registered metrics — balanced accuracy, F1 and ROC-AUC for classified stress detection; RMSE, MAE and R² for continuous prediction; reliability diagrams, the Brier score and prediction-interval coverage probability for calibration; and stress-detection lead time and per-season false-alarm rate for operational value — with literature-derived acceptance thresholds fixed in the validation protocol before the prospective season, and with the primary model frozen and its model card registered in the Primary model, benchmark and model card before the first field season. Freezing the model and pre-committing thresholds before the prospective test is the methodological device that makes the transferability claim honest.

Transferability is treated at three distinct levels rather than conflated. Temporal transfer is tested by the blocked unseen-year validation above; environmental transfer is tested by prospectively applying the frozen model at an independent commercial farmer field instrumented by the project with a meteorological station and soil sensors, supported by physiological, proximal, UAV and Sentinel observations (Objective O3), quantifying the research-to-commercial transfer gap and applying a limited, pre-specified recalibration only if transfer is incomplete, as captured in the Independent commercial-field validation dataset and the Prospective transferability, uncertainty and limited-recalibration report; and methodological/crop transfer is handled by explicitly separating a reusable decision-support core (data architecture, physiology-to-prediction workflow, uncertainty logic, sensing-scale integration and the irrigation-attention interface) from crop-specific components (physiological reference ranges, phenological interpretation, stress thresholds and calibration parameters), documented in the Spectral/UAV/Sentinel harmonisation and crop-transfer specification with explicit recalibration gates any later crop must pass. Processing tomato is the scientifically justified starting crop — chosen because roughly five heterogeneous seasons of data and established expertise exist for it — not the intended limit of the technology; the project builds and documents the methodology required for controlled transfer rather than claiming that a tomato-trained model can be applied unchanged elsewhere.

Operationalisation (Objective O4) follows the science rather than leading it. The pre-existing DrR - Digital Agronomist prototype is used as a research-to-application vehicle: only validated scientific components are incrementally incorporated into a crop-configurable web MVP that keeps crop-specific parameters explicit, delivered as the Crop-configurable DrR web MVP with validated processing-tomato module and evaluated for operational usability and interoperability by AgroVIR. The principle "the software follows the science, not the other way around" is a methodological constraint that protects the fellowship from becoming a software-development project.

**Identified challenges and how they are overcome.** The methodology names its own principal risks and builds the countermeasures into the workflow. (i) Archive heterogeneity and missingness: overcome by the common-variable matrix, an explicit missingness strategy and a defined effective statistical unit fixed before modelling. (ii) Optimistic generalisation from random splits: overcome by blocked, leakage-safe unseen-year validation and pre-registered metrics/thresholds. (iii) The research-to-field transfer gap: overcome by a frozen model, prospective commercial-field testing and a pre-specified limited-recalibration protocol, so that any performance drop is measured and reported rather than hidden. (iv) Fragility of UAV/hyperspectral campaigns: overcome by prioritising acquisitions around key physiological measurement dates and by retaining physiology and proximal sensing as the core pathway if individual UAV campaigns are missed. (v) Dependence on a single commercial validation site: overcome by a defined site-contingency ladder, in which a second independent commercial processing-tomato producer serves as a first-line, claim-preserving backup and a public-garden route serves as a measurement-only fallback with an explicitly downgraded transferability claim. (vi) The temptation to over-fit for accuracy: overcome by the parsimony-and-interpretability stance and by scoring operational value (lead time, false-alarm rate) alongside statistical fit.

### Integration of methods and disciplines to pursue the objectives

An interdisciplinary approach is essential here, not optional: the central challenge cannot be met by any single discipline, because it requires a physiological definition of stress, a rigorous data-science treatment of prediction and uncertainty, a remote-sensing treatment of scale, and an agricultural/operational treatment of decision relevance to co-exist within one workflow. FIELDWISE integrates four method families. Plant-stress physiology and agronomy supply the physiologically meaningful stress target, the corroborating endpoints and the judgement of whether model-derived signals track genuine plant responses; this strand is anchored in the HUN-REN ATK Plant Physiology and Metabolomics Department, whose head is a plant-stress physiologist, and in the processing-tomato experimental and archive base contributed by MATE. Agricultural data science supplies the parsimonious modelling, feature engineering, calibration, uncertainty analysis and leakage-safe validation design. Remote sensing and geoinformatics supply the hyperspectral/UAV-to-Sentinel scale-transition methodology that prevents leaf-, plot- and satellite-scale measurements from being treated as equivalent. Software engineering and operational farm-management expertise supply the translation of validated functions into a maintainable, interoperable prototype: Krumatic provides software development from project start, and AgroVIR provides requirements-oriented consultation from the outset and later operational and interoperability evaluation.

The integration mechanism is deliberately structured rather than assumed. The disciplines meet at defined methodological interfaces — the physiological target definition constrains the predictor set; the predictor set and validation protocol constrain the model; the scale-transition specification governs how proximal signals become field-scale inputs; and the reusable-core/crop-specific separation governs what is allowed to enter the DrR architecture. This is reinforced by a deliberately complementary two-way transfer of knowledge: the fellow contributes agronomy, plant protection, plant-stress physiology, physiological phenotyping, horticultural field experimentation, proximal spectral interpretation and the existing DrR concept, while the host and partners contribute advanced agricultural data science, robust modelling and uncertainty analysis, hyperspectral/UAV/EO integration, precision-agriculture workflows and research-to-software/industry translation. The remote-sensing, UAV and hyperspectral environment and a co-supervisory methodological strand for scale-aware EO interpretation are provided on the ELTE side as an associated partner, and the predictive-modelling/machine-learning methodological leadership is carried by a named ELTE-side team member. The result is an interdisciplinary design in which the fellow is the integrating agent who, by the end of the action, will have carried a scientific concept through biological definition, model development, unseen-condition validation, software implementation and industrial evaluation.

### Gender dimension and other diversity aspects

A sex/gender dimension in the *content* of the research is not relevant to FIELDWISE, and this conclusion follows directly from the nature of the research object rather than being an omission. The biological subject of study is the processing-tomato crop and its physiological water-stress response; the project collects no human or animal biological data, no health, biometric or special-category data, and no personal attributes for which sex or gender is an analytical variable. There is therefore no biological or physiological endpoint in the research on which a sex/gender analysis could operate, and introducing one would be artificial. In line with the guidance that this question concerns research content and not team composition, no gender-dimension claim is made about the scientific model.

Other diversity aspects are, however, taken into account where the research and innovation content actually touches people — namely in the design and evaluation of the decision-support output. Because the DrR web MVP and its irrigation-attention interface are intended for real growers, inclusive, user-centred design is treated as a methodological requirement: structured requirements consultation and usability, missing-data-behaviour and interoperability evaluation with AgroVIR and with participating farmers are used to ensure the tool serves users with differing farm sizes, differing degrees of digital literacy and differing operating contexts, rather than an idealised advanced user. The dissemination and uptake pathway is explicitly bilingual and cross-border, with Krumatic supporting Bulgarian farmer-facing uptake alongside the Hungarian validation and evaluation environment, so that the innovation is accessible across the two national grower communities the project works in. Where human participants provide feedback — grower requirements and the operational evaluation — participation is governed by informed consent and a right of withdrawal, and farmer and commercial data are minimised and processed in coded or anonymised form. These measures are the appropriate treatment of diversity for a project whose only human dimension is end-user engagement.

### Open science practices as an integral part of the methodology

Open science is embedded in the workflow rather than appended to it, under the governing principle "as open as possible, as closed as necessary". Several methodological choices are simultaneously open-science practices. The pre-registration of the stress target, feature-selection approach, metrics and literature-derived acceptance thresholds before the prospective season — fixed in the Stress-target, feature-selection and validation protocol — is a reproducibility and transparency commitment that guards against outcome-selective reporting. The primary model is documented with a model card in the Primary model, benchmark and model card, exposing its intended use, predictors, performance, calibration and known limitations. The evidence base itself is treated FAIR-by-design: the Harmonised database/metadata and variable-availability map produces documented, quality-controlled data and metadata, and methods, metadata and publications are made reusable wherever possible. The project relies on open Copernicus/Sentinel-2 Earth-observation data for its field-scale inputs, and results derived from commercially sensitive farmer or partner information are published only in aggregated, coded or anonymised form.

Open access to publications is planned: at least two high-quality peer-reviewed papers (physiologically grounded water-stress signatures; modelling, uncertainty and transfer from historical experiments to prospective commercial-field validation), with an optional third methods/application paper, are targeted for open-access dissemination, complemented by conference presentations, seminars and practitioner-facing demonstrations. Open science is also carried into training as a transferable-skills competence (research integrity, open science and FAIR practice, generative-AI literacy), so that the fellow consolidates these practices as part of the career transition. Data governance is handled honestly rather than naively: a background/foreground inventory is established at project start, and pre-existing DrR background, FIELDWISE scientific foreground, institutional datasets and partner-developed code are treated as separate rights layers, with potentially protectable foreground evaluated before public disclosure — the "as closed as necessary" side of the principle that legitimately balances openness against valorisation. Consistent with the standard MSCA requirement for FAIR data management and open science, a Data Management Plan will be produced as an early project deliverable, within the first six months of the action, detailing data types, standards, storage, sharing, access and long-term reuse arrangements and operationalising the FAIR and open-access commitments above across all work packages.

### 1.3 Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host

**A complementary supervisory team matched to the two pillars of the action.** FIELDWISE is a 30-month European Postdoctoral Fellowship (24 months at the host, M1–M24, plus a 6-month non-academic placement, M25–M30, under CC-07), and its supervision is structured around the two disciplinary pillars on which the science depends: plant-stress physiology and agricultural data science / Earth observation. Primary supervision is provided at the recruiting organisation and host, HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont (ATK), Martonvásár, by Prof. Tibor Janda, Head of the Plant Physiology and Metabolomics Department at the Agricultural Institute. His expertise — plant physiology, abiotic-stress (including drought) physiology and stress metabolomics — is exactly the competence the scientific spine of the project requires: he anchors the definition of the physiologically meaningful water-stress target, the judgement of whether model-derived and remotely sensed signals track genuine plant responses, and the physiological measurement programme. As head of an established department with extensive drought and abiotic-stress research, he directs a mature advanced-training environment and is positioned to supervise at the level the fellowship demands. The host's institutional capacity to deliver high-quality MSCA supervision is evidenced, not asserted: HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont coordinated and hosted the funded MSCA Individual Fellowship LANDRACES (752453, 2017–2019) and participates in Horizon Europe today (COUSIN, AI4SoilHealth, TUdi). A committed supervisory effort of approximately 2.5 person-months across the action underwrites substantive, recurring engagement rather than nominal oversight.

Co-supervision is provided by Prof. András Jung of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics — a specialist in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy and multisensor data fusion — who carries the hyperspectral/UAV-to-Sentinel scale-transition strand, the second methodological pillar, with a co-supervisory effort of approximately 2.0 person-months. As an associated partner, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) additionally contributes Dr. Roland Hollós as the named team member responsible for the predictive-modelling/machine-learning strand (heterogeneous agricultural-data integration, AI/ML approach selection, feature engineering, validation design, uncertainty analysis and model interpretation) and Dr. Zsófia Varga for practical UAV operation, flight planning and imaging-sensor deployment. The source scientific environment, Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE), contributes the longitudinal 2022–2026 processing-tomato archive and agronomic/irrigation expertise through Dr. Sándor Takács, with senior precision-agriculture and decision-support consultation from Prof. Gábor Milics. The result is a single fellow supported by named specialists covering every methodological interface the project crosses — physiological definition, modelling and uncertainty, sensing-scale transition, and operational translation — so that no strand of the interdisciplinary programme is left without expert guidance.

**Structured supervision and governance.** Supervision is delivered through a defined cadence rather than ad hoc contact: a weekly one-to-one meeting between the fellow and the supervisor; technical sessions with the co-supervisor through the EO-harmonisation strand and with the ELTE-side predictive-modelling team member through the modelling-intensive window, tapering outside them; a monthly written progress record held by the fellow; and a quarterly review against the Career Development Plan attended by both supervisors. A Project Steering Group chaired by the supervisor, with the fellow, the co-supervisor, the ELTE-side modelling team member and one named contact each from the data, software and placement partners, provides go/no-go oversight at defined steering points across the action, including a mid-placement review. Decision rights and a two-step, office-based conflict-resolution route are pre-defined, so that scientific, methodological, resourcing and access decisions each have a clear owner and escalation path. This governance is designed to give an experienced researcher returning to full-time research after a documented career break a stable, well-defined support structure while protecting her scientific independence.

**Planned training activities (scientific, management and transferable skills).** The training design is that of supervised practice on real project work, organised as three scientific strands and a transferable-skills programme, and it directly serves the call's expected outcomes of increased research and transferable skills, improved employability, and enhanced quality and sustainability of research training and supervision. Scientifically, the fellow is trained in (i) physiological water-stress interpretation, validation-parameter selection and phenotyping practice at the host under the supervisor; (ii) geoinformatics, field spectroscopy, hyperspectral/UAV methods, multisensor fusion and scale-aware EO interpretation in the Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) spatial-sensing environment under the co-supervisor and with UAV operations support; and (iii) heterogeneous-data integration, AI/ML-supported modelling, feature engineering, leakage-safe validation design and uncertainty analysis with the ELTE-side predictive-modelling team member. This addresses the fellow's one remaining competence gap — rigorous predictive modelling and model validation across time, sensing scales and environments — and completes her progression from plant physiologist/agronomist using digital tools to an independent Agricultural Data Scientist specialised in plant stress, Earth observation and decision-support systems. Management and research-management competences are built through leading the harmonisation, validation and MVP work and coordinating multi-partner data, instrument and field-site access. Transferable skills are trained explicitly and in line with the call's requirement to integrate digital, open-science, valorisation and integrity competences: research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; IP and exploitation; project management; and science communication. A teaching strand transfers an existing strength — approximately five years of university teaching in plant physiology and plant-stress physiology at the Agricultural University of Plovdiv — into the new discipline through short guest lectures, seminars and practical sessions at Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE) and, where institutionally possible, the Agricultural University of Plovdiv, feeding research results back into teaching. The whole plan is consolidated in the Career Development Plan, established jointly by both supervisors and the fellow and submitted early as an obligatory deliverable (Career Development Plan), and reviewed at defined steering points across the action, satisfying the call's Career Development Plan requirement.

**Two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host.** Because FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship, the relevant transfer is the two-way exchange between the researcher and the host and its associated partners; there is no outgoing phase and therefore no three-way construction. The transfer is deliberately complementary and bidirectional. The fellow brings into the host environment agronomy, plant protection, plant-stress biology, physiological phenotyping, horticultural field experimentation, proximal spectral interpretation and the existing DrR concept and multi-source data-integration experience — grounding that the modelling and EO strands need in order to be physiologically valid rather than merely statistically accurate. The host and partners provide, in return, advanced agricultural data science, robust modelling and uncertainty analysis, hyperspectral/UAV/EO integration, precision-agriculture workflows and research-to-software/industry translation. Concretely, the host contributes plant-stress-physiology supervision and institutional research integration; the associated Earth-observation partner contributes scale-aware sensing and the predictive-modelling strand; and the fellow contributes the biological and experimental grounding and the DrR application concept. This is a genuine exchange — the fellow strengthens the host's biological grounding and application reach while the host consolidates the fellow's data-science and EO competences — which is precisely the knowledge-transfer and R&I-capacity outcome the call seeks for participating organisations.

**Rationale and added value of the non-academic placement.** The proposal includes an integral, end-of-project non-academic placement (WP5 — AgroVIR Non-Academic Placement) at AgroVIR (M25–M30), included as an integral and separately evaluated part of the proposal in line with the call's optional up-to-six-month placement provision; no separate secondment is proposed. The placement supplies inter-sectoral competences the academic host cannot provide alone: operational model evaluation against a production farm-management information system, research-to-MVP translation, agricultural-software requirements engineering, interoperability assessment, user-centred decision support and exploitation planning. AgroVIR's added value is credible on operational grounds — its farm management information system is in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria, the two countries FIELDWISE works in — even though its track record is commercial rather than research-based, with no participation in EU-funded research projects. The placement is conducted mainly through remote collaboration with monthly face-to-face technical meetings, and is designed so that the fellow does not require access to proprietary customer databases or production systems: AgroVIR supplies protected, coded or anonymised extracts (for example coded field identifiers) sufficient for the agreed evaluation tasks (MVP usability, missing-data behaviour, interoperability, and finalisation of FMIS-integration requirements, an exploitation roadmap and career-transfer outputs). It is supervised by Miklós Maróti, whose managing-director experience in agricultural digitalisation and farm-management systems is the basis for the supervision argument, with a committed partner effort of approximately 3.0 person-months. Crucially, the placement deepens an established collaboration rather than opening a cold one: AgroVIR is consulted from M1, so requirements feedback shapes the MVP throughout WP4 before the formal evaluation begins. Ownership of placement results follows the grant-agreement default, vesting in HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont as beneficiary acting through the fellow, with a written placement agreement between the fellow, HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont and AgroVIR concluded before the placement begins to confirm this allocation and the access terms to the fellow's DrR background. By completion, the fellow will demonstrably have carried a scientific concept through biological definition, model development, unseen-condition validation, software implementation and industrial evaluation — a distinctive, cross-sectoral competence profile relevant to universities, research organisations, precision-agriculture and irrigation-technology companies, EO/geospatial organisations and FMIS providers.

The status of the forward-looking supervision and placement commitments is stated transparently: the supervisor's and co-supervisor's formal acceptance of their seats and committed effort, the ELTE-side representation of the predictive-modelling team member and the instrument-access arrangement, the named data-partner contact, and the placement arrangement, supervisor, effort and IP allocation are operator-declared working assumptions to be confirmed in partner writing before the action starts; the identities, institutional roles and infrastructure on which they rest are confirmed on public and partner-authored evidence.

**1.4 Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills**

**A profile deliberately matched to the two pillars of the action.** The experienced researcher, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova — who published before 2020 under the name Rositsa Cholakova-Bimbalova — brings a professional profile that is closely and demonstrably matched to FIELDWISE, because the project was conceived around the two competence axes on which her career already sits: established depth in plant-stress physiology and agronomy, and a rapidly consolidating capability in agricultural data science and Earth observation. Appropriateness here is not a general assertion of excellence but a specific fit — each strand of the scientific programme draws on experience she already holds, and the single element she does not yet hold at the required level is precisely the element the fellowship is designed to supply. Her existing experience therefore maps onto the project by design rather than by coincidence.

**Established scientific foundation in plant-stress physiology and agronomy.** Her doctoral and academic record supplies the physiological grounding on which the project depends. She holds a PhD in Plant Physiology (2020, Agricultural University of Plovdiv, under Prof. Dr. Andon Vassilev), preceded by BSc and MSc degrees in Plant Protection, giving her the agronomy-and-plant-protection base that the crop-facing work of the action requires. From 2015 to 2020 she was Assistant Professor in Plant Physiology and Plant Stress Physiology at the Agricultural University of Plovdiv — approximately five years of teaching and supervised research directly in the discipline that anchors the physiologically meaningful water-stress target at the heart of objective O1 (Harmonise the heterogeneous 2022-2026 MATE archive and define a physiologically meaningful water-stress target). Since 2024 she has been Chief Assistant Professor and plant-physiology researcher at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute (MVCRI), where her current abiotic-stress work — including the drought and salinity strand of the ZEMDKT 17 programme in Solanum lycopersicum and the tomato multi-stress SolGenSys action — keeps her scientifically active in exactly the crop and the stress domain that FIELDWISE studies. This is the competence that allows her to judge whether a model-derived or remotely sensed signal tracks a genuine plant response rather than an unvalidated spectral proxy — the discriminating judgement the whole validation chain rests on.

**Horticultural field experimentation and physiological measurement practice.** Alongside the theoretical grounding, she brings hands-on horticultural field experimentation, physiological phenotyping and proximal spectral interpretation. This experimental competence is directly appropriate to the archive-harmonisation, stress-target definition and physiological-validation activities of the project, and it is the biological grounding she contributes into the host environment as her half of the two-way knowledge transfer, ensuring the modelling and Earth-observation work remain physiologically valid rather than merely statistically accurate.

**An already-underway transition into data science and Earth observation.** The second pillar — the one the fellowship helps her consolidate — is already substantially underway, which is what makes the transition credible rather than aspirational. Her applied data-science experience includes a period as a Data Analyst at KPMG Global Hungary (Python, R, basic machine learning, Power BI and work over large datasets) and earlier agricultural-market analysis using survey and database tools; it is embodied most concretely in DrR - Digital Agronomist, her self-financed, pre-existing research tool, which she already uses in her MVCRI research as a sensor, Earth-observation and data-integration environment (not, at this stage, a validated advisory product). Her Earth-observation and remote-sensing competence is evidenced through a coherent set of recent, verifiable activities rather than resting on a publication record: a COST Short-Term Scientific Mission (CA22136 PANGEOS) hosted at MATE in 2025, Erasmus+ staff mobilities to MATE and the University of Novi Sad in 2025-2026, an Erasmus master's internship at ELTE in 2026, an A1/A3 UAV pilot licence, an in-progress second MSc in Environmental Engineering, and membership of three COST Actions (PANGEOS, AI4Insect and REcrop). The proposal is explicit and honest that the Earth-observation half of her profile rests on this practical, mobility- and licence-based experience rather than on deep publication output — of her nine recorded publications only a small number touch remote sensing, all recent and as a contributing author — and this candour is itself appropriate to an interdisciplinary transition still in progress.

**Precise alignment with the project, and the one remaining gap.** Taken together, her existing profile maps onto every strand of FIELDWISE except one, and that single remaining gap is the explicit rationale for the fellowship. Her competence base already covers physiological definition, agronomy and plant protection, horticultural experimentation, proximal sensing, practical UAV/EO practice and applied data handling; what it does not yet include at the level the science demands is rigorous predictive modelling and model validation across time, sensing scales and environments. FIELDWISE is therefore a consolidation of an already-established interdisciplinary trajectory — from plant physiologist and agronomist using digital tools toward an independent Agricultural Data Scientist specialised in plant stress, Earth observation and decision-support systems — rather than a change of field, and it is structured so that this one gap is closed through supervised practice on the project's own modelling and validation work (the training design that delivers this is set out in section 1.3 and is not repeated here).

**Professional maturity, timing and integrating capacity.** She is, in addition, a returning researcher: following a documented full-time-parenting career break of just over 34 months (2021-2024, in Budapest), she has re-entered research with clear momentum, and the break does not count against the MSCA research-experience window — making the timing of the fellowship apt for an experienced researcher re-establishing a full-time research trajectory. Her teaching record — approximately five years of university lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English, including for Erasmus students, with supervision of Bachelor's theses — supplies the communication and knowledge-transfer skills on which the action's teaching and dissemination activities draw. The combined profile makes her well placed to be the integrating agent the project needs: a single researcher able to carry one physiologically defined concept through biological definition, model development, unseen-condition validation, software implementation and industrial evaluation — which is exactly the distinctive, cross-sectoral competence the fellowship is built to produce.

The selected call is HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01 (MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026).
The action is a European Postdoctoral Fellowship with a 6-month non-academic placement extension.
The project duration is 30 months (24-month fellowship phase at the host plus a 6-month placement).
The host/recruiting organisation is HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont (ATK), Martonvásár, Hungary.

The primary supervisor at HUN-REN ATK is Prof. Tibor Janda.
The programme is organised around four objectives O1-O4 whose canonical titles are reproduced verbatim.

The central challenge is whether a water-stress signal found in processing tomato stays biologically meaningful across seasons/scales, survives prospective field validation, and can be encoded in a crop-configurable decision-support framework.
The objectives close three focused gaps: physiological grounding of stress indicators, transferability across unseen conditions/scales/crops, and irrigation decision relevance.

Each objective is defined by concrete measurable outputs (e.g. QC-controlled common-variable matrix; ranked predictor set, model card and crop-transfer specification; prospective validation dataset and unseen-environment benchmark; web MVP with validated tomato module).
Objectives are anchored to dated deliverables — D1.1/D1.2/D2.2 (month 14), D2.1 (month 3), D3.1/D3.2 (month 18), D4.1 (month 24), D5.1/D5.2 (month 30) — enabling verification.

Model evaluation uses pre-registered metrics under blocked unseen-year validation with literature-derived acceptance thresholds fixed in D1.2 before the prospective season, and the primary model is frozen and its model card registered before the first field season.
O1/O2 are grounded in the heterogeneous 2022-2026 MATE processing-tomato archive of physiological, soil, meteorological and proximal spectral observations.

DrR - Digital Agronomist is the fellow's pre-existing, self-financed research tool (a sensor/EO monitoring and data-integration tool, not a validated advisory product) used as the research-to-application vehicle.
O3 is validated prospectively at an independent commercial farmer site instrumented by the project (meteorological station and soil sensors), with a defined site-contingency ladder.
O4 operationalisation relies on Krumatic software development from project start and AgroVIR requirements consultation followed by the M25-M30 industrial evaluation/placement.
Extension to additional cultivars/Bulgarian conditions is placed after the action as a post-MSCA replication route through MVCRI, with no in-action MVCRI effort claimed.

Ambition beyond the state of the art is expressed as seven concrete transitions (stress proxy to physiological target; internal fit to blocked unseen-year to independent commercial-field validation; proximal to UAV to Sentinel-2 scale bridge; standalone model to DrR web MVP with AgroVIR evaluation; tomato prototype to crop-configurable framework, etc.).

The project explicitly refuses four common assumptions (vegetation index equals water stress; proximal and satellite indices interchangeable; internal cross-validation proves field transferability; one tomato-trained model transfers unchanged to other crops).
The methodological novelty is a physiologically grounded validation framework rather than a new algorithm; the stance is parsimony and interpretability without a deep-learning dependency.

The framework separates a reusable, crop-configurable decision-support core from crop-specific physiological/phenological/calibration components, with explicit crop-transfer validation/calibration gates.
The methodology reuses the existing 2022-2026 processing-tomato archive as its primary evidence base rather than mounting a new campaign, harmonised into a QC-controlled common-variable matrix (O1).
A physiologically meaningful water-stress target is defined and fixed before modelling, replacing spectral-proxy stress definitions.
The predictive framework is parsimonious, interpretable and uncertainty-aware and deliberately avoids a deep-learning dependency.
The work rests on four testable hypotheses H1-H4 (physiological signature, transferability, scale-transition, operational relevance) as underpinning assumptions.
The model learns the relationship between operational predictors (soil-water, weather, spectral/EO) and an independently measured physiological water-stress target.
Model selection and evaluation use blocked, leakage-safe unseen-year temporal validation.

Evaluation uses pre-registered metrics (balanced accuracy, F1, ROC-AUC; RMSE, MAE, R2; reliability diagrams, Brier score, PICP; lead time, false-alarm rate) with literature-derived acceptance thresholds fixed in the validation protocol before the prospective season.
The primary model is frozen and its model card registered in the Primary model, benchmark and model card (D2.1, month 3) before the first field season.
Transferability is treated at three distinct levels: temporal (unseen-year), environmental (research-to-commercial field), and methodological/crop transfer.

The frozen model is validated prospectively at an independent commercial farmer field instrumented with a meteorological station and soil sensors, with a limited-recalibration protocol if transfer is incomplete (O3).
A reusable decision-support core is explicitly separated from crop-specific biological/calibration parameters, with a documented crop-transfer specification and recalibration gates.
