sub_sections.title: Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development
sub_sections.content:
Sub-section 2.1 — Credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development

Starting point and the competence gap the fellowship closes. Dr. Rositsa Cholakova enters FIELDWISE as an accomplished plant physiologist and agronomist, holding a BSc/MSc in Plant Protection/Agronomy, a PhD in Plant Physiology, approximately five years of university teaching and research in plant stress physiology, and an expanding technical profile in remote sensing, hyperspectral sensing, UAV applications, GIS and agricultural data analysis. The measures proposed here are credible precisely because they are targeted: FIELDWISE is designed around the one competence gap that stands between this profile and full independence in a fast-growing field — rigorous predictive modelling and model validation across time, sensing scales and environments. By closing that gap, the fellowship completes a coherent progression from a plant physiologist/agronomist who uses digital tools into an independent Agricultural Data Scientist specialised in plant stress, Earth observation and decision-support systems. This is the researcher-facing outcome the whole action is engineered to deliver, and it is what directly serves the call's expected outcome of an increased set of research and transferable skills leading to improved employability and career prospects within academia and beyond (EO-01) and its corresponding expected impact (EI-01). It is not asserted as a slogan: it is operationalised by the Career Development Plan and the inter-sectoral placement set out below, and it is measured by the project's own career KPI.

The Career Development Plan as the governing skills-development instrument. The central measure is a Career Development Plan, delivered as an early, formal project deliverable (D1.3 Career Development Plan, due month 3) and established jointly by the supervisors and the researcher, satisfying the mandatory scope requirement that such a plan be agreed jointly and submitted at the beginning of the action (SR-08). It is not a one-off document: it is signed by both supervisors and the fellow, and it is revisited at five defined steering/review points across the fellowship (M6, M14, M18, M24 and M27), so that training and career needs are re-assessed against progress rather than fixed at the outset. The plan binds together research objectives (O1 to O4), an explicit training-and-career-needs strand delivered as supervised practice, a structured transferable-skills curriculum, a teaching strand, publication planning, and an open-science engagement commitment framed as "as open as possible, as closed as necessary". This structure gives the evaluator a concrete, reviewable governance object rather than a promise, and it is the instrument-level mechanism through which FIELDWISE aligns the researcher's working conditions with the principles of the European Charter for Researchers.

The transferable-skills curriculum. The Career Development Plan itemises a transferable-skills set matched to the call's mandatory training requirement (SR-07): research integrity; open science and FAIR practice; generative-AI literacy; grant writing; intellectual property and exploitation; project management; and science communication. These competences are not taught in the abstract — they are exercised on the project's own material. FAIR and open-science practice are exercised in harmonising and documenting the five-season data archive and in publishing methods and metadata; generative-AI literacy and modelling rigour are exercised in the interpretable, uncertainty-aware modelling work; IP and exploitation skills are exercised in maintaining the background/foreground rights inventory and preparing the exploitation route; and grant-writing and project-management skills are exercised through the fellow's leadership of a multi-partner, single-researcher action. This design means each transferable skill is anchored to a deliverable the fellow actually produces, which is what makes the skills-development claim credible rather than generic.

Discipline-specific scientific skills and the two-way transfer of knowledge. The core scientific up-skilling is delivered through a defined, complementary two-way transfer. The fellow contributes agronomy, plant protection, plant physiology, plant-stress biology, physiological phenotyping, horticultural field experimentation, proximal spectral interpretation and the existing DrR concept; the host and partners provide advanced agricultural data science, robust modelling, uncertainty analysis, hyperspectral/UAV/Earth-observation integration, precision-agriculture workflows and research-to-software/industry translation. Supervision is anchored at the recruiting organisation, HUN-REN ATK, by Prof. Tibor Janda, head of the Plant Physiology and Metabolomics Department, whose remit covers the physiological water-stress target, the physiological validity of model outputs and the physiological measurement programme. The associated partner ELTE supplies two named methodological strands: Prof. András Jung as co-supervisor for geoinformatics, field spectroscopy, hyperspectral/UAV methods, multisensor fusion and scale-aware Earth-observation interpretation; and Dr. Roland Hollós as the ELTE-side team member responsible for the predictive-modelling/machine-learning component (heterogeneous data integration, AI/ML-supported modelling, feature engineering, validation design, uncertainty analysis and model interpretation). Practical UAV and hyperspectral training is provided in the ELTE spatial-sensing environment, with Dr. Zsófia Varga supporting mission planning, sensor operation and data acquisition. This spread of named expertise across physiology, Earth observation and machine learning is exactly the interdisciplinary breadth the fellow needs to consolidate the Agricultural Data Scientist profile, and it directly instantiates the new mind-sets and approaches forged through international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience that the call expects (EO-02).

Inter-sectoral employability: the non-academic placement. Employability beyond academia is addressed through a concrete, integral measure rather than an aspiration: a six-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR in the final phase of the fellowship (M25-M30), included as an integral and evaluable part of the proposal under the additional-placement provision (SR-06). The placement supplies competences the academic host cannot provide alone — operational model evaluation, research-to-MVP translation, agricultural-software requirements, interoperability assessment, user-centred decision support and exploitation planning. Its credibility rests on continuity: AgroVIR is consulted from M1, so the placement deepens an established collaboration rather than opening a cold one, and by completion the fellow will have demonstrably carried a scientific concept through biological definition, model development, unseen-condition validation, software implementation and industrial evaluation — a distinctive profile for both academic and non-academic agricultural data-science careers. The placement is conducted mainly through remote collaboration with monthly face-to-face technical meetings, and is supervised by Miklós Maróti, Managing Director of AgroVIR, whose experience in agricultural digitalisation and farm-management systems is directly relevant to the fellow's intended career direction. This inter-sectoral exposure is the mechanism by which FIELDWISE contributes to the call's expected impact of stimulating knowledge transfer and expanding career opportunities by promoting career moves between sectors and organisations through the non-academic placement incentive (EI-05).

Teaching, communication and profile-building. The plan preserves and re-purposes an existing strength: building on approximately five years of prior university teaching in Plant Physiology and Plant Stress Physiology at the Agricultural University of Plovdiv (2015-2020, including syllabus design, lecturing and examining in Bulgarian and English and Bachelor's supervision), the fellow will seek short guest lectures, seminars and practical sessions at MATE and, where institutionally possible, the Agricultural University of Plovdiv, transferring an established teaching capability into the new discipline. Scientific visibility is built through at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions (P1 on physiologically grounded water-stress signatures; P2 on modelling, uncertainty and the transfer from historical experiments to prospective commercial-field validation), with a third methods/application paper if the independent dataset supports it, alongside conference presentations and practitioner-oriented demonstrations. These activities enhance the networking and communication capacities the call expects a fellow to gain.

Expected contribution of the skills to the future career. The combined effect of these measures is a research-to-operation competence portfolio that is deliberately broad in its employability. FIELDWISE gives the fellow end-to-end experience from multi-year scientific evidence, through leakage-safe modelling and independent commercial-field validation, to a web-accessible MVP and industrial assessment. This portfolio is explicitly relevant to universities, European research organisations, precision-agriculture and irrigation-technology companies, Earth-observation/geospatial organisations, crop-phenotyping groups and farm-management-information-system (FMIS) providers — a spread that spans academic and non-academic destinations and therefore materially improves the researcher's career prospects inside and outside academia. Because the Career Development Plan is agreed early, reviewed at five steering points and signed by both supervisors and the fellow, the skills-development pathway is auditable and adaptive; and because working-condition alignment with the European Charter for Researchers is evidenced at instrument level by that plan and the documented supervision and training arrangements (no institutional HR award is claimed for HUN-REN ATK, as its status has not been established), the credibility of the measures rests on committed, verifiable arrangements rather than on unverified accreditation. Taken together, the plan, the interdisciplinary supervision architecture and the inter-sectoral placement form a single, coherent instrument for consolidating the fellow's target profile and demonstrably enhancing her employability within academia and beyond.

sub_sections.title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
sub_sections.content:
Sub-section 2.2 — Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

Overall strategy and proportionality to a single-researcher action. FIELDWISE treats dissemination, exploitation and communication as one continuous, planned strand rather than an end-loaded afterthought. The work plan carries a dedicated cross-cutting dissemination/exploitation strand alongside the training/two-way-transfer strand and the management/Open Science/IP strand, running across the whole action and resourced from the fellow's cross-cutting person-month allocation. Because this is a single-researcher fellowship executed by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, every measure below is deliberately sized to what one fellow, supported by the host HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont and the associated and partner organisations, can credibly deliver and sustain — a focused set of high-quality outputs and well-targeted audience actions rather than an over-scaled campaign. The whole strand is governed by the Open Science principle "as open as possible, as closed as necessary": methods, metadata and publications are made reusable wherever possible, while any potentially protectable foreground is evaluated before public disclosure. This proportionate, front-to-back design is what allows the modest resource of a single postdoctoral action to still generate scientific, practitioner-facing and industrial impact.

Target groups. The plan addresses five distinct groups, each with a matched channel: (i) the scientific and professional research community in plant-stress physiology, agricultural data science, remote sensing/Earth observation and precision agriculture; (ii) growers, farm advisors and the wider agricultural sector, particularly in the two countries FIELDWISE works in, Hungary and Bulgaria; (iii) the agricultural-software and farm-management-information-system (FMIS) industry, together with precision-agriculture and irrigation-technology companies, Earth-observation/geospatial organisations and crop-phenotyping groups, as the exploitation-relevant audience; (iv) students and the higher-education community; and (v) the general public and policy-relevant audiences, framed through the project's contribution to SDG 2, SDG 6, SDG 12 and SDG 13. Naming the groups explicitly lets each activity be judged on fit rather than on volume.

Dissemination to scientific and professional audiences. Scientific dissemination is built around at least two high-quality peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship: P1 on physiologically grounded water-stress signatures derived from the heterogeneous MATE archive, and P2 on modelling, uncertainty and the transfer from historical experiments to prospective commercial-field validation; a third methods/application paper on multi-scale UAV/Sentinel operationalisation and DrR is prepared if the independent dataset supports it. These are complemented by conference presentations and by seminars in the MATE, HUN-REN and ELTE environments. Dissemination is delivered under Open Science discipline in line with the call's training requirement: open access to publications, and FAIR, reusable methods and metadata, including the registered model card of the Primary model, benchmark and model card and the Stress-target, feature-selection and validation protocol, and the harmonised datasets and variable-availability map where institutional permissions allow. Crucially, the project commits to reporting transfer honestly — the Prospective transferability, uncertainty and limited-recalibration report (due month 18) treats any performance drop under prospective validation as a scientific result to be quantified rather than hidden — which is itself a form of high-integrity dissemination. This directly serves the call's expected outcome of enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers (EO-03) and the corresponding expected impact of increased and broadened R&I impact (EI-02), and it feeds the stronger R&I capacity and better knowledge transfer among participating organisations (EI-05) through the model card, the Spectral/UAV/Sentinel harmonisation and crop-transfer specification (due month 14) and the two-way transfer between the fellow and the ATK/ELTE/MATE environments.

Communication to practitioners, students and the public. Communication is deliberately widened beyond research audiences. The fellow will deliver practitioner-oriented demonstrations of the stress and uncertainty outputs; Krumatic supports Bulgarian farmer-facing dissemination, demonstration and uptake of the MVP, providing a concrete channel into the Bulgarian grower community. As an operator-preserved commitment, the project targets one public field demonstration with farmers and one public-facing article per year. Only if it is formally established and scientifically suitable, a public-facing demonstration at the planned Szentendre Skanzen model Bulgarian garden would link traditional horticultural knowledge with modern environmental sensing; this is stated conditionally and carries no unconditional promise. Teaching-linked communication — short guest lectures, seminars or practical sessions at MATE and, where institutionally possible, the Agricultural University of Plovdiv — feeds research results back into higher education. Together these activities address broadened public engagement (EI-03) and the feedback of results into teaching (EI-06), while remaining sized to a single fellow's realistic reach.

Exploitation plan. Exploitation is anchored in a tangible research-to-application vehicle: the crop-configurable DrR web MVP with validated processing-tomato module (due month 24), which provides a concrete route from validated research to external testing while preserving the distinction between the fellow's pre-existing DrR background and the FIELDWISE foreground. Because the MVP is completed before the M25-M30 placement, the non-academic placement at AgroVIR is genuine evaluation and transfer rather than first build: it yields the AgroVIR operational/interoperability assessment (due month 30) covering MVP inputs, usability, missing-data behaviour, decision outputs, workflow compatibility and interoperability requirements, and the Post-MSCA FMIS integration and exploitation roadmap (due month 30), which names the required interfaces, the exploitation route and the post-fellowship steps. The architecture is crop-configurable by design: within the action, validation is confined to processing tomato, and the Spectral/UAV/Sentinel harmonisation and crop-transfer specification defines the transferable core components, crop-specific parameters, minimum validation datasets and recalibration gates any later crop addition must pass — so exploitation beyond tomato is presented as a scientifically controlled pathway, not an unsupported universalisation. Economic value is deliberately not expressed as an invented EUR/ha or fixed water-saving promise; instead the project quantifies the measured quantities — irrigation water applied, water productivity, yield and marketable yield, quality indicators, intervention timing and warning lead time — from which later economic value can be assessed. A defined post-MSCA replication route through MVCRI transfers and re-validates the outcomes on additional tomato cultivars under Bulgarian production conditions as knowledge transfer outside the 24-month work plan (no in-action MVCRI effort is claimed). This inter-sectoral, cross-border exploitation logic instantiates the call's expected impact of stimulated innovation and knowledge transfer and expanded career opportunities through the non-academic placement incentive (EI-05) and reinforces the fellow's employability across academic and non-academic destinations (EI-01). The delivery of the reachable web MVP, the completion of the external AgroVIR evaluation and the definition of the integration path give the plan three concrete, verifiable exploitation checkpoints.

Intellectual-property management and foreseen protection measures. IP is managed on a separate-rights-layers doctrine established at the outset. At project start, HUN-REN ATK, ELTE, MATE, Krumatic, AgroVIR and the fellow establish an inventory of relevant background datasets, software, code, methods and other assets, and this background/foreground inventory is maintained throughout the action as an explicit task and used to define the post-MSCA exploitation route. Four rights layers are kept distinct and each documented before the action starts: the fellow's pre-existing DrR background; the FIELDWISE scientific foreground; institutional datasets; and Krumatic-developed code. The fellow's DrR background is stated to have been initiated and developed independently using her own time and personal financial resources, with no MVCRI ownership position — a position to be confirmed in writing and hardened by a dated background declaration and version inventory before the action starts. Protection measures are proportionate and staged: potentially protectable foreground is evaluated before public disclosure under the "as closed as necessary" limb; MATE data are used only for the approved scientific purposes of FIELDWISE under institutional data-use conditions to be documented before the action starts, and any use of MATE-derived models or institutional assets in a future marketable product is subject to a separate legal and institutional data-rights/IP assessment before commercial exploitation. Code-IP terms for the FIELDWISE code (ownership or sufficient exploitation rights) are to be settled in a Krumatic development agreement concluded before the action starts. For the placement, ownership of results is to follow the grant-agreement default, vesting in HUN-REN ATK as beneficiary acting through the fellow, with a written placement agreement between the fellow, HUN-REN ATK and AgroVIR — concluded before the placement begins — confirming this allocation and the access terms to the DrR background; the placement itself is conducted mainly through remote collaboration, with AgroVIR supplying only protected, coded or anonymised data extracts (for example "Field X" identifiers) so that no access to proprietary customer databases or production systems is required. Farmer and AgroVIR operational information is minimised and coded/anonymised where appropriate, and results are published only in aggregated, coded or anonymised form. Several of these arrangements (MATE data rights, the placement IP allocation and the placement data arrangement) rest on operator declarations pending partner writing and are presented as such rather than as settled fact; the IP framework nevertheless gives the evaluator a complete, layered protection design rather than a gap.

Concrete actions during and after the project, and overall proportionality. During the action, the measures are embodied in named, resourced activities: the continuous dissemination/exploitation strand; the maintained background/foreground/IP inventory; structured AgroVIR requirements consultation from month 1; the DrR web MVP and its pre-placement usability/interoperability dossier; annual public-facing communication; and the placement's operational evaluation. After the action, continuity is secured by the Post-MSCA FMIS integration and exploitation roadmap, the MVCRI Bulgarian replication route, the crop-transfer specification enabling later crop modules after crop-specific validation, and publications appearing during or shortly after the fellowship. All of this is scaled to a single-researcher MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship: a compact, high-quality output set with clearly matched target groups and verifiable checkpoints, delivering scientific, practitioner and industrial impact without over-committing the resources of one fellow.

sub_sections.title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
sub_sections.content:
Sub-section 2.3 — The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

How the results make a difference beyond the immediate scope. FIELDWISE is a single-researcher action on one development crop, but its contribution is deliberately engineered to reach past that immediate scope along three connected axes — scientific, agricultural/environmental and technological/economic — with a defined European and societal relevance layered on top. The unifying mechanism is that the project does not merely build another crop-stress model; it builds and prospectively tests a validation framework in which operationally obtainable data streams are judged against independent plant-level ground truth and challenged under both unseen-year and genuinely new commercial-field conditions. The result that outlives the action is therefore methodological knowledge: which physiological water-stress relationships survive the transition from proximal measurements toward UAV and Sentinel-2 field-scale monitoring, and which components of the modelling and decision workflow are genuinely reusable beyond the development crop. This is what converts a processing-tomato study into a methodological basis for later crop-by-crop extension across irrigated high-value horticulture — a scientifically controlled pathway rather than an unsupported universalisation from a single crop. Its importance is that it addresses the exact failure mode that limits digital agronomy today: models that fit retrospective data but are never shown to hold under scale change, new seasons and real production settings.

Scientific impact and its magnitude. The scientific contribution is concentrated in three durable, citable objects: the Primary model, benchmark and model card, which reports calibration, uncertainty and blocked unseen-year performance; the Spectral/UAV/Sentinel harmonisation and crop-transfer specification, which enumerates the transferable core components, crop-specific parameters, minimum validation datasets and recalibration gates any later crop must pass; and, above all, the Prospective transferability, uncertainty and limited-recalibration report (due month 18), which quantifies the transfer gap from research experiments to an independent commercial field and states any performance drop honestly rather than hiding it. The magnitude of this contribution is best measured not by a single accuracy figure but by the fact that it delivers a reusable, uncertainty-aware protocol and an openly reported transfer result — a form of high-integrity science that is directly reusable by other groups and that strengthens the research capacity and knowledge transfer of the participating HUN-REN ATK, ELTE and MATE environments through the documented two-way transfer and the planned peer-reviewed publications. This is the project's principal route to the call's expected impact of increased and broadened research and innovation impact (EI-02) and of increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations (EI-05).

Agricultural and environmental impact — credible magnitude with disciplined honesty. FIELDWISE begins with processing tomato precisely because roughly five seasons of heterogeneous scientific observations (2022-2026) already exist, while the intended application domain is irrigated high-value horticulture. Critically, the project makes no fixed-percentage water-saving promise, because real savings depend on crop, cultivar, soil, weather, growth stage, irrigation system and the management action actually taken. What the project provides for magnitude is credible, bounded, literature-referenced context: comparable published studies demonstrate water-saving effects in the approximate 8–30% range under specific strategies — for processing tomato, plant-and-soil monitoring has been reported to reduce irrigation by around 30% versus empirical farmer management and by around 7.5% versus ET-based scheduling in a two-year field trial (Carucci et al. 2023), and early-stage controlled deficit has achieved roughly 25% water saving without statistically significant yield loss while poorly timed deficits reduced yield (Badr et al. 2026). These are stated as bounded context only, never as a FIELDWISE promise; they establish that the magnitude at stake is material and that the water–yield trade-off must be quantified rather than assumed. The project's own claimed value is therefore expressed as correct stress detection, warning lead time, uncertainty honesty, usability and irrigation-attention relevance. Prospective water-saving quantification is claimed only to the extent the commercial farmer-field irrigation-treatment arrangement actually supports it; where it does not, FIELDWISE reports detection, lead-time and uncertainty outcomes together with measured yield and quality. This disciplined framing is itself part of the importance of the contribution: it gives evaluators a defensible magnitude signal without overclaiming.

Technological and economic impact and its magnitude. The economic and technological contribution is anchored in a tangible research-to-application vehicle rather than a paper concept: the crop-configurable DrR web MVP with validated processing-tomato module (due month 24) provides a concrete route from validated research to external testing, while preserving the distinction between the fellow's pre-existing DrR background and the FIELDWISE foreground. Because the architecture is crop-configurable — reusable data-ingestion, uncertainty, visualisation and irrigation-attention components separated from crop-specific parameters — the same investment can support additional crop modules after crop-specific validation, multiplying the reach of a single fellowship's output. The magnitude of the economic contribution is deliberately not fabricated as an invented EUR/ha or fixed water-saving figure; instead the project measures the quantities from which later economic value can genuinely be assessed — irrigation water applied, water productivity, yield and marketable yield, quality indicators, intervention timing and warning lead time. The route to real-world uptake is made concrete by the AgroVIR operational/interoperability assessment (due month 30) and the Post-MSCA FMIS integration and exploitation roadmap (due month 30), which name the required interfaces, the exploitation route and the post-fellowship steps, with Krumatic supporting software implementation and Bulgarian farmer-facing uptake. This inter-sectoral chain is the mechanism by which FIELDWISE contributes to stimulated innovation, knowledge transfer and expanded career opportunities through the non-academic placement incentive (EI-05).

European and societal relevance and its scale. The societal magnitude is bounded and evidenced rather than rhetorical. Eurostat reports fresh vegetables cultivated over approximately 2.0 million hectares in the EU in 2023, and about 0.7 million EU farms cultivating fresh vegetables in the 2020 census — an indication of the scale of the horticultural domain in which scientifically transferable, plant-based irrigation decision support could ultimately matter, presented explicitly as a potential application domain and not as an immediate addressable market. Bulgaria supplies concrete downstream context for the project's cross-border replication logic: about 35.6 thousand hectares of main vegetable area and roughly 128 thousand tonnes of tomato in harvest 2024. The combination of Hungarian scientific and industrial environments, a real farmer validation setting, Bulgarian software and dissemination links through Krumatic, and a defined post-MSCA replication and re-validation route through MVCRI provides a realistic pathway toward wider reuse, contributing particularly to SDG 2, SDG 6, SDG 12 and SDG 13. This cross-border pathway also broadens public and practitioner engagement with the research (EI-03) through practitioner-oriented demonstrations and farmer-facing communication.

Importance, credibility and proportionality of the contribution. The importance of FIELDWISE's contribution rests on three features that keep magnitude claims credible. First, every quantified magnitude is either drawn from published literature and labelled as bounded context, or measured from the project's own prospective data — the proposal deliberately avoids inventing water-saving or economic figures. Second, the contribution is auditable: an eleven-KPI set (K1–K11) is defined so that each indicator measures something the project actually controls and delivers and each traces to a named deliverable, so the magnitude of delivery can be checked rather than asserted. Third, the design converts an apparent weakness — a single fellow on a single crop — into strength, because the transferable core, the crop-transfer gates and the post-MSCA MVCRI route extend the reach of the work beyond the 24-month scientific programme without over-committing the resources of one fellowship. Taken together, the scientific protocol and honest transfer result, the disciplined agricultural/environmental magnitude context, the concrete research-to-operation economic vehicle, and the evidenced European/Bulgarian scale give the evaluator a contribution whose magnitude is significant precisely because it is credible, controlled and reusable beyond the immediate case.

sub_sections.content:
## 3.1 Quality and effectiveness of the work plan, assessment of risks and appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages

### Overall structure of the work plan

FIELDWISE is implemented as a single-beneficiary MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship (European Fellowship) hosted by HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont, with a total duration of 30 months: a 24-month fellowship period at the host (months 1-24) followed by a 6-month non-academic placement (months 25-30) under CC-07. Because this is a single-researcher action, the experienced researcher (Dr. Rositsa Cholakova) personally executes the scientific content of every work package; the partner organisations contribute supervision, data, instruments, software engineering and the operational evaluation environment as in-kind support. The work plan is deliberately compact — four work packages, eleven deliverables and six milestones — so that the effort concentrates on scientific substance rather than on managing a large consortium.

The four work packages follow the project's causal chain from evidence to operation, so that each package supplies a validated input to the next:

- **WP1 — Data Harmonisation, Stress Definition and Model Development** (lead: HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont). Harmonises the heterogeneous five-season MATE archive, fixes a physiologically meaningful water-stress target, and develops, evaluates and freezes the primary, parsimonious water-status model. It produces the Career Development Plan (D1.3), the Primary model, benchmark and model card (D2.1), the Harmonised database/metadata and variable-availability map (D1.1), the Stress-target, feature-selection and validation protocol (D1.2) and the Spectral/UAV/Sentinel harmonisation and crop-transfer specification (D2.2).
- **WP3 — Independent Commercial-Farmer Prospective Validation** (lead: the independent commercial-farmer validation site). Applies the frozen model prospectively at an instrumented, independent commercial field and quantifies the transfer gap, delivering the Independent commercial-field validation dataset (D3.1) and the Prospective transferability, uncertainty and limited-recalibration report (D3.2).
- **WP4 — DrR Web MVP, Co-development and Exploitation Preparation** (lead: КРУМАТИК ЕООД). Co-develops the crop-configurable web MVP that carries the validated processing-tomato module and prepares the post-MSCA exploitation route, delivering the Crop-configurable DrR web MVP with validated processing-tomato module (D4.1) and the Pre-placement technical/usability requirements dossier (D4.2).
- **WP5 — AgroVIR Non-Academic Placement** (lead: AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság). Evaluates the MVP operationally during the non-academic placement and finalises the operational assessment and integration roadmap, delivering the AgroVIR operational/interoperability assessment (D5.1) and the Post-MSCA FMIS integration and exploitation roadmap (D5.2).

Six milestones gate progress: MS1 (Historical knowledge base and target definition complete), MS6 (Primary model frozen and registered), MS2 (Model and scale-transition framework ready for final prospective assessment), MS3 (Independent real-world transferability quantified), MS4 (MVP ready for industrial placement evaluation) and MS5 (Industrial evaluation and placement completed). Each milestone carries a verifiable achievement criterion — for example, MS6 is met only when the primary water-status model parameters are fixed and the model card (D2.1) is registered with recorded performance metrics before the first prospective field season begins, and MS3 is met when the frozen model has been applied prospectively and the transfer gap quantified with an uncertainty estimate in D3.2.

### Timing of the work packages and their components

The schedule is front-loaded on the science and back-loaded on operation, with two work packages running in parallel through the middle of the action:

- **WP1** runs from the outset to month 14. Its opening tasks — auditing the archive, defining the common-variable matrix, selecting the physiological stress target and predefining blocked temporal validation (T1.1-T1.5) — complete ahead of the month-3 model freeze. MS1 confirms the historical knowledge base and target definition before that freeze; the primary model is then developed and frozen, delivering D1.3 and D2.1 at month 3 and triggering MS6. The harmonisation and crop-transfer strand (T2.4-T2.6) continues to month 14, delivering D1.1, D1.2 and D2.2 and reaching MS2.
- **WP3** begins after the month-3 model freeze and runs across the growing season(s) to month 18, when D3.1 and D3.2 are delivered and MS3 quantifies real-world transferability. Securing written field access, installing the meteorological station and soil sensors, and conducting the coordinated physiological, proximal, thermal and UAV campaigns precede the prospective application of the frozen model.
- **WP4** runs in parallel from month 1 to month 24. Structured AgroVIR consultation is used from project start (T4.4) and software development proceeds from the outset, so that validated data and model functions are migrated incrementally into the web MVP; D4.1 and D4.2 are delivered at month 24 with MS4.
- **WP5** is the 6-month non-academic placement at AgroVIR, months 25-30, delivering D5.1 and D5.2 at month 30 and closing the action at MS5.

The inter-package dependencies are explicit and were normalised in scheduling. The single strict finish-to-start dependency is WP4→WP5 (and, at task level, T4.3→T5.1): the MVP delivered at MS4 (month 24) must exist before the placement evaluation can begin, and the WP-level constraint is feasible because WP4 ends at month 24 and WP5 starts at month 25. The remaining inter-WP links (WP1→WP3, WP1→WP4, WP3→WP4) are data_input dependencies that pass information without enforcing strict temporal ordering, which is what allows WP4 to co-develop concurrently rather than waiting for WP3 to finish. The critical path is therefore: freeze the primary model (T2.3) → apply it prospectively and quantify the transfer gap (T3.5) → migrate validated core functions toward the MVP (T4.3) → operational evaluation (T5.1) → MS5. Freezing the model before any field season (MS6) is a deliberate design choice that keeps the WP3 validation genuinely out-of-sample and removes the risk of hindsight fitting.

### Gantt chart (months elapsed)

```
Months elapsed (1 -> 30)      1   3       6       9      12      14  16  18      21      24  25      27      30
WP1  Data Harmon./Model    |=============================|                                                  (M1-14)
       D1.3,D2.1 @3   MS1(pre-3)  MS6 @3                D1.1,D1.2,D2.2 @14 / MS2 @14
WP3  Prospective Valid.               |===========================|                                        (after M3 freeze -> M18)
                                          D3.1,D3.2 @18 / MS3 @18
WP4  DrR Web MVP           |===================================================|                            (M1-24)
       AgroVIR consult. + Krumatic dev. from M1          D4.1,D4.2 @24 / MS4 @24
WP5  AgroVIR Placement                                              |===================|                  (M25-30, non-academic placement)
                                                                        D5.1,D5.2 @30 / MS5 @30

Legend:  |===| work-package span      D#.# deliverable (canonical due month)      MS# milestone
Note:    This is a single-beneficiary European Fellowship: the mobility element is the WP5 non-academic
         placement at AgroVIR (months 25-30); there are no secondments. Bars are positioned on months
         elapsed and anchored to confirmed deliverable due months (3, 14, 18, 24, 30) and the confirmed
         fellowship/placement structure (M1-24 fellowship + M25-30 placement = 30 months).
```

### Appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages

The researcher's effort is 30 person-months of full-time work over the 30-month action, distributed to match where the intellectual weight of the project lies: WP1 (merged data-harmonisation and model-development package) 9.0 PM, WP3 6.6 PM, WP4 6.0 PM, WP5 5.4 PM, and 3.0 PM cross-cutting (training and Career Development Plan activity, dissemination, open-science and project management), totalling 30.0 PM. WP1 carries the largest share because it holds the scientific core — harmonising a heterogeneous five-season archive and building an interpretable, uncertainty-aware model are the most demanding tasks. WP3 is the second-heaviest because prospective field validation is campaign-intensive. WP4 is spread thinly but continuously across 24 months, reflecting incremental co-development rather than a single build. WP5 concentrates on the placement months. This profile is consistent with a single-researcher action in which the fellow is the sole executor of scientific content.

Partner effort is contributed in kind and is stated as an operator-declared commitment pending each partner's written confirmation: the host supervisor 2.5 PM, the ELTE co-supervisor 2.0 PM, AgroVIR 3.0 PM (the largest partner figure, as the only partner hosting the fellow during the placement), MATE 2.4 PM and КРУМАТИК ЕООД 1.5 PM. These figures are scaled to well-defined roles — supervision cadence, data preparation and archive access, software development, and operational evaluation — and none represents a dependency that could block the researcher's own critical-path work.

### Mechanisms to assess and mitigate risks

Risk is managed through a grouped ten-row register (R01-R10) covering research, measurement, operational and data-rights/administrative risks, each rated for likelihood (L) and impact (I) and paired with a concrete mitigation:

- **Research and modelling risk.** R01 — historical MATE variables differ among years (L=M, I=H): use an explicit year-by-variable matrix, harmonise only defensible common variables and retain year-specific measurements as secondary information. R02 — limited effective biological sample size (L=M, I=H): use repeated-measure/hierarchical structure, conservative feature reduction and parsimonious modelling with no deep-learning dependency. R07 — prospective performance drops (L=M, I=H): treat transfer loss as a scientific result, quantify uncertainty and apply limited transparent recalibration rather than hiding the gap.
- **Measurement and observation risk.** R03 — farmer site lacks modern monitoring infrastructure (L=H, I=M): install a project meteorological station and soil sensors before the campaign and define maintenance and data-quality responsibilities. R05 — ELTE instrument access or timing is constrained (L=M, I=H): use a written equipment/operation schedule, prioritise key physiological dates and retain physiology/proximal sensing as the core pathway if individual UAV campaigns are missed. R06 — field geometry or clouds limit Sentinel-2 interpretation (L=H, I=M): use Sentinel only where valid pixels support field-scale inference and rely on UAV/proximal observations for finer scales.
- **Operational and partner risk.** R04 — primary farmer access changes or is interrupted (L=M, I=H): secure written access (task T3.1) and follow a contingency ladder — first activate an identified second commercial processing-tomato producer (which, if it meets the measurement protocol, preserves the independent commercial-field transferability claim), and only if that also fails activate the Szentendre Skanzen model-garden route, which preserves the physiological measurement programme but does not substitute for commercial-field transferability evidence, so the transferability claim is then explicitly downgraded and reported as such. R08 — web development is delayed (L=M, I=M): develop incrementally from the existing prototype, keep scientific deliverables primary and prioritise validated core functions over feature breadth. R09 — the placement host cannot provide proprietary/customer data (L=L, I=M): design the placement around usability/interoperability requirements and protected, coded extracts, so unrestricted customer-system access is not a project dependency.
- **Data-rights and administrative risk.** R10 — MATE-derived assets carry commercial restrictions (L=M, I=H): use them for approved research only, maintain a background/foreground inventory and conduct an institutional data-rights/IP assessment before any commercial exploitation.

The overarching risk philosophy is that transfer loss is a scientific result to be measured, not concealed: a performance decrease under prospective validation is quantified, its uncertainty stated, and only limited, transparent recalibration applied. This philosophy is embedded in the plan itself through the model-freeze-before-validation sequencing (MS6 ahead of WP3).

Risks are assessed and escalated through the project's governance structure: a Project Steering Group reviews progress at the milestone points and issues a go/no-go verdict on the milestones MS1-MS5, so that no downstream work package proceeds on an input that has not passed its verifiable criterion. Day-to-day scientific risk is handled by the researcher with the primary supervisor (Prof. Tibor Janda) through the regular supervision cadence, with unresolved items escalated within the host and, where relevant, through the owning partner's access agreement. This combination — a critical path with a single strict dependency, milestone-gated go/no-go review, a pre-registered validation protocol, and a contingency ladder for the one field-access dependency that is not fully under the project's control — keeps the action robust while remaining honest about what is confirmed and what still depends on partner writings to be finalised.

## 3.2 Quality and capacity of the host institutions and participating organisations, including hosting arrangements

### The host: HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont

FIELDWISE is a single-beneficiary MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowship. The sole beneficiary, recruiting organisation and host is HUN-REN Agrartudomanyi Kutatokozpont, a public research organisation of the HUN-REN Hungarian Research Network, located at Brunszvik u. 2, 2462 Martonvásár, Hungary (registered PIC 866599553). It is not a higher education institution but a research centre, and the fellowship is anchored in its Agricultural Institute. The host has a documented capacity to recruit and develop MSCA fellows: it previously hosted and coordinated the funded MSCA Individual Fellowship LANDRACES (H2020 grant 752453, Standard European Fellowship, 2017-2019), and its current Horizon Europe participations (COUSIN, AI4SoilHealth and TUdi) evidence an active, funded research environment. This prior MSCA hosting record means the institution already operates the recruitment, mentoring, financial-administration and reporting machinery that an incoming fellow relies upon.

Scientifically, the host supplies exactly the environment FIELDWISE needs at its core. It provides the computational and data-processing environment required for multi-source data integration and predictive modelling, with access to the wider HUN-REN research infrastructure for the computationally intensive analyses the work plan calls on, and strong, well-established expertise in plant phenotyping. The primary supervisor's unit — the Plant Physiology and Metabolomics Department at the Agricultural Institute — is a physiological-validation environment with extensive experience in drought and abiotic-stress physiology, which underwrites the physiological water-stress target that distinguishes FIELDWISE from spectral-proxy approaches. Modelling and data-integration collaboration continues with the host's Department of Crop Production. The primary supervisor, Prof. Tibor Janda, heads the Plant Physiology and Metabolomics Department and brings plant physiology, abiotic-stress (including drought) physiology and stress metabolomics; his identity and departmental headship are established from his curriculum vitae and the host capacity record. His formal acceptance of the primary-supervisor seat, and the associated supervision effort, remain to be confirmed in the host's written hosting confirmation and are therefore stated here as a commitment pending that writing rather than as settled fact.

### Hosting arrangements: integration and support services

The host will act as recruiting organisation and beneficiary, hosting the fellow at the Agricultural Institute in Martonvásár with a dedicated workspace, full integration into the hosting group, administrative support, and access to institutional training, and it will continue these arrangements through the six-month non-academic placement (months 25-30). Support services available to the researcher include the host's research-administration and grants function, its computational and data infrastructure, library and IT services, and its research-integrity and data-protection functions (the host's data-protection function will be consulted before any personal data are processed in the web MVP). Integration is operationalised through the supervision cadence set out in Section 3.1 — weekly one-to-one meetings with the primary supervisor, a monthly written progress record, and quarterly reviews against the Career Development Plan (D1.3) — so that the fellow is embedded in the day-to-day scientific life of the department rather than hosted at arm's length. These hosting arrangements and support services are the host institution's own facilities and commitments; consistent with §12.2, they are recorded as an operator-declared commitment that converts to confirmed on the host's written hosting confirmation naming the Part A signatory and grants-office contact. The host's PIC (866599553) is active on public registers, which is sufficient to submit; the recent HUN-REN institutional transformation is flagged for a Part A verification with the host's grants office and does not affect the hosting capacity described here.

Because FIELDWISE is a European Fellowship arising from an intra-EU move (Bulgaria to Hungary), there is no outgoing Third Country host and no separate return host to outline: the Global Fellowship two-host requirement does not apply. The six-month non-academic placement at the placement host is an extension under constraint CC-07 within the same European Fellowship, not a Global Fellowship outgoing phase. The mobility profile, researcher development and career-development dimensions of the host arrangement are set out in the Excellence sub-sections and are not repeated here.

### Participating organisations and associated partners

As a single-beneficiary action, FIELDWISE has no consortium of co-beneficiaries; the participating organisations act as associated partners linked to the beneficiary and as one collaborating validation environment. Their infrastructure, logistics and facilities are set out in full in Part B-2 Section 5; the summary below establishes that each brings a capacity the work plan genuinely depends on.

**Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE)** is an associated partner providing the remote-sensing, UAV/hyperspectral and geoinformatics environment, based in its Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics in Budapest (the Multisensor-Drone-Image Fusion research environment and the GIS and Remote Sensing Laboratory). Its confirmed instrument inventory — a DJI Matrice 350 RTK industrial drone with Zenmuse L1 (LiDAR/RGB), P1 (45 MP photogrammetry) and H20T (thermal) payloads, an Ultris S5 hyperspectral camera and a Cubert CUVIS laboratory hyperspectral package, together with licensed ArcGIS, ENVI and MATLAB, open geospatial tools (Google Earth Engine, QGIS, SNAP), and high-performance computing for large-scale geospatial analysis — is precisely the equipment the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel scale-transition strand relies on. The co-supervisor, Prof. András Jung (Professor, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics), carries this remote-sensing, hyperspectral-imaging, field-spectroscopy and multisensor-fusion expertise, and Dr. Zsófia Varga supports the fellow's UAV data acquisition, flight planning and sensor operation. ELTE's published output (recent DOI-verified Earth-observation and agricultural remote-sensing papers) evidences the quality of this environment. Two things about ELTE's involvement are stated as commitments pending written confirmation rather than as settled facts: ELTE's continuation as an associated partner (its written associated-partner agreement is evidence-grade and awaited), and the instrument-access arrangement under which the fellow conducts or co-conducts measurements with these platforms scheduled around key physiological dates. Under the same standing, Dr. Roland Hollós participates on the ELTE side as the named team member responsible for the predictive-modelling/machine-learning component (AI/ML approach selection, heterogeneous-data integration and model interpretation); his identity and modelling profile are established, while his ELTE-side representation basis awaits ELTE's written confirmation. The co-supervisor's acceptance of the co-supervision role is likewise a pending commitment.

**Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem (MATE)** is an associated partner (Institute of Horticultural Sciences, PIC 891269563) and the source scientific environment. It supplies the heterogeneous 2022-2026 processing-tomato archive that makes processing tomato the development crop, together with the experimental and validation instrument base: TDR and capacitive soil-moisture sensors at 15 and 30 cm, stomatal resistance/conductance equipment, SPAD chlorophyll meters, VIS-NIR (approx. 325-1075 nm) and VIS-NIR-SWIR (approx. 350-2500 nm) leaf spectroradiometers, meteorological monitoring, leaf-surface temperature measurement and CWSI assessment tools. The archive is described by season, variable class and treatment, and MATE additionally brings precision-agriculture and decision-support consultation (Prof. Gábor Milics). MATE's grant of rights and access to the 2022-2026 archive, under institutional data-use conditions to be documented before the action starts, is stated as a commitment pending MATE's written data-use permission; it does not block the work plan, which is designed to draft against a stated (not fabricated) access position.

**КРУМАТИК ЕООД** is an associated partner and the software-development and Bulgarian-uptake organisation: a Bulgarian technology and digital-solutions company (EIK 201511899, established 2011, Sofia), with software-implementation and systems-integration experience including previous involvement in deploying the placement host's farm-management platform in Bulgaria. It provides continuous developer support from project start — improving the DrR prototype, implementing validated data/model functions and the crop-configurable architecture, and migrating the validated core toward the web MVP — plus later-stage Bulgarian farmer-facing dissemination and uptake, a role deliberately distinct from the placement host's operational-evaluation function. Its legal identity and role are established from partner-supplied registry data; its SME status, its effort and the openly stated absence of any ownership/employment relationship with the fellow or other partners are stated as commitments pending the company's confirmation, and code-IP terms are a pre-grant development-agreement action rather than a proposal fact.

### Non-academic placement host: AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság

The operational evaluator and non-academic placement host is AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság (AgroVIR Kft.), a Hungarian SME founded in 2007 and seated in Budaörs, which develops and operates a cloud-based farm management information system. Its confirmed organisational profile is directly relevant to FIELDWISE's research-to-operation ambition: the platform is in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, and its Hungarian and Bulgarian footprints match the two countries in which FIELDWISE works. This gives the fellow a genuine industrial evaluation environment for the validated MVP that the academic host cannot provide alone — operational model evaluation against a production FMIS, agricultural-software requirements practice, interoperability assessment, user-centred decision-support design and exploitation planning — which is why the placement is the inter-sectoral element of the fellowship. The placement work content is well defined (evaluation of MVP inputs, usability, missing-data behaviour and decision outputs; interoperability assessment; monthly technical reviews; and finalisation of FMIS-integration requirements and the exploitation roadmap), delivering the AgroVIR operational/interoperability assessment and the Post-MSCA FMIS integration and exploitation roadmap in WP5 — AgroVIR Non-Academic Placement.

The placement arrangement is stated as a commitment pending the company's written confirmation: it is conducted mainly through remote collaboration with monthly face-to-face technical meetings, the fellow works with the AgroVIR product development team responsible for the FMIS platform, and — importantly for feasibility and data protection — the fellow does not require access to proprietary software, customer databases, office infrastructure or computing equipment, because AgroVIR provides the information and data extracts needed for interoperability testing in protected, coded or anonymised form (for example, 'Field X' identifiers). The placement supervisor is Miklós Maróti, Managing Director of AgroVIR, whose experience in agricultural digitalisation and farm-management systems supports evaluation of the MVP's stress and irrigation outputs within practical workflows; his name, title and the supervision arrangement are stated as commitments pending AgroVIR's written confirmation. The company's track record is commercial rather than scientific — it declares no participation in EU-funded research projects — and this is stated openly in the prescribed form rather than converted into a research claim. AgroVIR holds no PIC yet; because it appears in Part A as the placement host, registration is a submission-time action (its legal name, address and tax number are all recorded) and is not a work-plan dependency.

### Collaborating validation environment and post-fellowship route

The independent commercial-farmer prospective validation site is a collaborating validation environment, not a beneficiary or associated partner: an unnamed independent commercial farmer in Hungary, introduced through the fellow's established professional relationship and deliberately left unnamed as a recorded operator decision. It provides realistic crop husbandry and field-management conditions; because it does not already operate the monitoring infrastructure the prospective validation requires, FIELDWISE installs an automated meteorological station and soil sensors, and the fellow retains responsibility for the scientific measurements, protocol, quality control and synchronisation. The farmer's written field access — site availability, permission for sensor installation, agreed irrigation-treatment implementation and routine crop management — is stated as a commitment to be secured before the campaign (task T3.1). As set out in the risk treatment in Section 3.1, a contingency ladder protects this single field-access dependency: an identified second independent commercial processing-tomato producer serves as a first-line, claim-preserving backup, and only if that also fails is the Szentendre Skanzen model-garden route activated as a measurement-only backup, at which point the commercial-transferability claim is explicitly downgraded and reported as such. The Skanzen environment is a confirmed contingency option that is never presented as a guaranteed second experiment.

Finally, Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute — Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив, a scientific institute of the Bulgarian Agricultural Academy in Plovdiv — is retained as the post-MSCA replication and transferability route and sits on no work-package month line during the action. Keeping the full Bulgarian replication outside the 24-month scientific work plan protects feasibility while preserving a concrete, named route for subsequent replication, local recalibration and extension under Bulgarian vegetable-production conditions, together with joint publications, proposals, mobility and teaching. In sum, the host provides a funded, MSCA-experienced research environment with the physiological and computational capacity at FIELDWISE's core; the associated partners supply the remote-sensing instruments, the historical data and instrument base, and the software-development capability; and the non-academic placement host supplies a genuine industrial FMIS environment for operational evaluation — a set of organisations whose facilities and capacities are individually necessary and jointly sufficient for the work plan, with every forward-looking commitment honestly separated from what is already established.
